Researchers study caddisfly silk gene evolution and its potential for bioadhesive development
V. F. Frost
Caddisflies, known for spinning sticky silk to build protective cases in freshwater streams, are the focus of new genetic research reported on Jul. 7 by University of Utah scientist Russell Stewart and Brigham Young University biologists. The team examined a net-spinning species native to Utah, Arctopsyche grandis, focusing on the H-fibroin gene that produces the main protein in caddisfly silk.
Stewart said, “It’s an incredibly detailed look at how nature does polymer chemistry. We looked at the main silk protein from 18 individual caddisflies from the same species in two populations very close together. The heterogeneity in those genes was remarkable.” According to Stewart, this research provides insight into how much the silk gene varies among individuals living in two nearby but separate wild populations near BYU’s Provo campus.
The findings were published June 3 in Molecular Biology and Evolution. Co-author Paul Frandsen said, “We started to look into the genes involved in silk production because of emerging techniques, especially now with genetic engineering, to make prototypes for bio-inspired materials. The first step is to try to understand gene function. Russell’s early work was really foundational to understanding exactly how the protein was folding and how it was adapted to life underwater.”
The study found a surprising amount of diversity: 18 specimens carried 24 different versions of the H-fibroin gene, with some resulting in fibers up to 25% longer or shorter than others. Frandsen said, “It’s a bit of a paradox because the protein is ultra-diverse, but the features that make it diverse are very constrained… This is one of the most interesting evolutionary stories I’ve seen, and it does have implications for designing a bioadhesive material.”
Caddisflies belong to Trichoptera—close relatives of moths and silkworms—and diverged about 270 million years ago from their common ancestor with silkworms. Their adhesives can function underwater—something human-made adhesives struggle with—which could lead researchers toward new materials for medical or engineering use.
The underlying research received funding from organizations including the National Science Foundation and included contributions from students Ashlyn Powell and Gabriela Jijon as well as scientists at several museums.
